definition: A set of three algorithms: key generation, signing with a private key and verifying with the matching public key. RSA-PSS, ECDSA, Ed25519 and ML-DSA are signature schemes.
example: Ed25519 is a signature scheme with 32-byte public keys and 64-byte signatures.

definition: The key-generation step of a cryptographic scheme: it produces a fresh key pair (or secret key) from secure randomness. Weak randomness here makes every later operation weak.
The public half of a signing key pair: anyone holding it can check signatures, but it cannot create them.

A simplified signature construction where the message is first hashed to a short digest and the digest is signed. Real schemes define their own exact hashing and encoding, so follow the scheme rather than building this yourself.

A 2008 attack in which researchers used an MD5 chosen-prefix collision to obtain a CA-signed certificate whose signature was also valid for an intermediate CA certificate they controlled, letting them issue trusted certificates.
A whole number greater than 1 divisible only by 1 and itself. A conventional two-prime RSA modulus multiplies two large secret primes; general RSA formats can support more factors.

Producing a new message/signature pair accepted under a target public key without the authorised signing key. Under the usual chosen-message security goal, the message must not be one already submitted to the signing oracle; replaying a previously returned signature is not a new-message forgery.

Encoding added before a cryptographic operation for a specified scheme. RSA encryption and signature encodings have different purposes and security requirements; block-cipher padding instead fills a partial block.
RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme: RSA signature padding that adds a random salt and has a security proof. TLS 1.3 requires it whenever an RSA key signs the handshake.

Two attacks by Daniel Bleichenbacher on RSA PKCS#1 v1.5. The 1998 attack uses a server that reveals padding errors as an oracle to decrypt RSA ciphertexts; the 2006 attack forges signatures against sloppy parsers when the public exponent is 3.
example: The 2017 ROBOT study found the 1998 attack still worked against many major TLS servers.

definition: Java's and Android's cryptographic random-number API. A 2013 Android flaw made it repeat outputs, so some Bitcoin wallet apps reused ECDSA nonces and had their keys and funds stolen.
The twisted Edwards form of Daniel Bernstein's Curve25519, used by Ed25519 signatures; X25519 key agreement uses the same curve in Montgomery form.

An implementation designed to avoid secret-dependent control flow and memory-access patterns observable through timing. This reduces specified side channels; it does not guarantee immunity to every physical, compiler or platform attack.

RSA with a 2,048-bit modulus, whose fixed-width signatures are 256 bytes. NIST key-management guidance associates this size with roughly 112-bit classical security; applicable protocol and policy requirements still determine acceptability.

Standards for Efficient Cryptography 1, which specifies elliptic-curve cryptographic schemes and encodings. A compressed prime-field point includes its x-coordinate and a byte identifying the appropriate y-coordinate parity.
example: A P-256 point is 65 bytes uncompressed and 33 bytes compressed.

definition: Distinguished Encoding Rules: a strict binary encoding for ASN.1 data that gives exactly one encoding per value, so signatures over it are reproducible. Certificates are DER-encoded.

Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (FIPS 204, 2024), standardised from CRYSTALS-Dilithium: NIST's main post-quantum signature scheme. Keys and signatures are kilobytes rather than tens of bytes.
example: ML-DSA-65 has 1,952-byte public keys and 3,309-byte signatures.

definition: NIST's 2023 Digital Signature Standard. It specifies RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA (including Ed25519) signatures for US government use.

Microsoft’s technology for signing software with a publisher certificate and checking signed-file integrity. Whether a signature is checked, trusted or required before execution depends on the file type and platform policy.

Android application package, a signed distribution format for applications. Updates normally require signing continuity, but supported signing-key upgrade and rotation mechanisms can establish authorised successor keys.
A Git commit or tag carrying a cryptographic signature over its signed data. Verification establishes a relationship to a signing key; identifying the author needs a trusted binding of that key.
The field in a JWT header naming the signing algorithm. Libraries that trusted it let attackers choose "none" or switch RS256 to HS256; verifiers must enforce the expected algorithm instead.

DomainKeys Identified Mail: an email signing mechanism that authenticates selected headers and a canonicalised body hash under a domain’s DNS-published public key. The signing domain need not equal the visible From domain.

aliases: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance
definition: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance, specified in RFC 9989. It evaluates whether successful SPF or DKIM authentication aligns with the message’s Author Domain and communicates domain-owner policy and reporting preferences; receiver handling can apply local policy.

The signed response an authenticator returns when logging in with WebAuthn or a passkey: a signature over the authenticator data and a hash of the client data, which includes the server's challenge and the origin.

A W3C standard for signing parts of XML documents, used by SAML. In signature-wrapping attacks the signed element is moved and an unsigned one inserted, so the application reads data the signature never covered.

An XML statement about a subject, such as authentication or attributes, used in SAML identity systems. Assertions can be signed directly or protected within another signed protocol message; a NameID identifies a subject and is not the whole assertion.
Converting data to one agreed exact byte representation before signing or comparing it, so equivalent forms (different whitespace or attribute order) give the same bytes.

A signed token binding a data hash to a time under a timestamping authority’s policy. It can support evidence that data existed by that time; continued acceptance after compromise also depends on trustworthy timing, chain validation and relying-party policy.
Any system that will sign whatever an attacker submits. A compromised server allowed to call an HSM's sign operation becomes one: the key never leaves, but the attacker gets valid signatures.

The standard certificate format (profiled for the internet in RFC 5280): a signed document binding a subject name to a public key, with an issuer, a validity period and extensions, all signed by a certificate authority.
example: A TLS server certificate for shop.example.com contains its SAN list, its public key and the issuing CA's signature.

definition: Public key infrastructure: the certificate authorities, policies, trust stores and revocation systems that decide who may vouch for which public keys and how relying parties check them.

A certificate authority whose key may serve as a directly trusted anchor. Root certificates are commonly self-signed and distributed through trust stores; offline HSM custody and restricted signing are common operational designs rather than the definition of a root.

A certificate authority certified by another CA rather than directly used as the relying party’s trust anchor. It may issue further CA or end-entity certificates within its constraints; recovery from compromise requires relying parties to reject the compromised authority.

An end-entity certificate for a server, client or workload rather than an issuing CA. Its CA status is false or not asserted as permitted by the profile, so a valid leaf signature alone does not authorise it to issue certificates.

A chain of certificates from a trust anchor to a leaf that passes every check in RFC 5280: signatures, validity dates, CA flags, path length, name constraints, key usage and policy. Signatures alone are not enough.
Finding a usable chain from a leaf to a trusted root when several candidate issuer certificates exist, for example because of cross-signing. Poor path building caused outages when old roots expired.

A collection of trust anchors an application, browser or operating system accepts as starting points for validation. A chain to one anchor is necessary under that trust model, but application identity checks and other acceptance policy must also pass.
A public key (usually a root certificate) that a relying party trusts directly, without further proof. Path validation starts from it.
Abstract Syntax Notation One: a language for describing data structures, used to define certificates, keys and many security protocols. It is encoded to bytes with rules such as DER.
A text wrapping for keys and certificates: base64-encoded DER between lines such as -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----. The name comes from the old Privacy-Enhanced Mail standard.

The DER-encoded “to be signed” fields of an X.509 certificate: serial number, issuer, validity, subject, public key and extensions. The signature authenticates these bytes under the signature and hash security assumptions; an unauthorised modification should fail verification.

The party that signs and vouches for a credential. For a certificate it is the CA named in the Issuer field, whose own certificate supplies the key that verifies the signature; for a token it is the service that created and signed it.

The inclusive notBefore and notAfter interval checked for certificates in a validated path; trust-anchor acceptance is a separate local policy. Public TLS leaf certificates issued from 15 March 2026 have a 200-day maximum, falling to 100 days on 15 March 2027 and 47 days on 15 March 2029 under the CA/Browser Forum schedule.

A Common Name attribute in an X.509 distinguished name, often written CN. Current service-identity guidance and public-browser matching use appropriate subjectAltName entries rather than the Common Name for server-name verification.

Subject Alternative Name: an X.509 extension carrying typed identities such as DNS names, IP addresses, email addresses or URIs. A relying application chooses the permitted identity type and matching rules for its protocol.
example: A SAN list of shop.com and www.shop.com covers both names; *.shop.com covers one level of subdomain.

definition: An optional field in an X.509 v3 certificate that carries meaning such as allowed names, CA status or key usage. An extension marked critical must be understood and enforced, or the certificate rejected.

An X.509 extension indicating whether a certificate’s key may act as a CA. When present, pathLenConstraint bounds the number of non-self-issued intermediate CA certificates below it in a valid certification path, excluding the end entity.
The certificate extension restricting what the key may do, such as keyCertSign (sign certificates) or digitalSignature.

Extended Key Usage: an X.509 extension restricting a key to listed purposes such as TLS serverAuth or clientAuth. Applications enforce the relevant usages and their profile; an absent extension and anyExtendedKeyUsage require policy-specific handling.

A CA certificate extension restricting permitted or excluded names in subsequent certificates of a path. Constraints apply to the name forms they cover and to enforcing clients; a DNS restriction alone does not automatically constrain every other identity type.
Authority Information Access: a certificate extension giving the URL of the issuer's certificate and of the OCSP responder. Some clients use it to fetch a missing intermediate.
Certificate revocation list: a list of revoked certificate serial numbers, signed and published by the CA. Clients download it to check whether a certificate has been withdrawn early.

Withdrawing acceptance of a certificate before expiry, for example after a key leak. Clients can obtain status through CRLs, OCSP, stapling or browser-managed data. Freshness, coverage and soft-fail versus hard-fail policies vary; revocation does not alter the signature bytes.

Online Certificate Status Protocol: signed status responses for identified certificates, with freshness information. A direct client query can disclose the checked certificate and associated browsing information to the responder.

Sending a signed certificate-status response through the TLS server instead of requiring each client to retrieve it from a responder. This avoids that direct lookup’s privacy and latency costs when applicable, but freshness, coverage and failure policy still matter.

A policy that does not reject solely because revocation status is unavailable, assuming the other checks pass. An attacker may exploit blocked status retrieval; it does not mean an explicitly revoked result is accepted.
A policy that rejects when required revocation status cannot be established. This avoids accepting an unknown status but can cause outages when fresh usable evidence is unavailable.
Chrome's compact list of selected high-priority revocations, pushed to browsers through updates instead of being fetched per certificate. It does not cover every revoked certificate.

Mozilla’s compressed revocation-status mechanism for covered publicly trusted TLS certificates, enabling local checks. Firefox 142 release notes document its revocation deployment; coverage and fallback rules remain product policy.

Signed certificate timestamp: a CT log’s signed promise to incorporate a certificate within its maximum merge delay. Applicable browser CT policies specify the required count, diversity and eligibility of logs for covered public TLS certificates.
A version of a certificate carrying a poison extension, submitted to CT logs before final issuance so the resulting SCTs can be embedded in the real certificate.
A CA issuing a certificate it should not have, for example to someone who does not control the domain, or one that breaks the Baseline Requirements.
Microsoft's former web browser. In 2002 it was shown not to check Basic Constraints, so any leaf certificate could sign valid-looking certificates for other sites.
Certificate signing request: a message containing your public key and requested names, signed with your private key to prove you hold it. You send it to a CA to get a certificate.
The standard format for certificate signing requests (RFC 2986).

Checking that a certificate requester controls the relevant domain names using an approved validation method. It does not establish the requester’s legal organisation or the trustworthiness of the website.

Organisation Validation: certificate issuance that includes checks on the subscriber’s legal organisation as well as domain authorisation. This category does not itself determine stronger encryption than domain-validated issuance.

Extended Validation: a public-certificate category with specified additional legal-entity and requester checks. It does not itself increase cryptographic strength; browser presentation is a separate, changing product policy.

Automatic Certificate Management Environment (RFC 8555): a protocol supporting automated certificate issuance and renewal through account-authenticated requests and identifier-control challenges. Fully unattended operation requires the client to satisfy those challenges automatically.
The test an ACME CA sets to prove domain control: publish a value derived from a random token and your account key over HTTP, in DNS or in a special TLS certificate.
The ACME challenge where you serve the key authorization at http://<domain>/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token> on port 80. It proves control of one host and cannot be used for wildcard certificates.
The ACME challenge where you publish a digest of the key authorization in a TXT record at _acme-challenge.<domain>. It is the only Let's Encrypt method for wildcard certificates.
The ACME challenge (RFC 8737) where the server presents a special self-signed certificate on port 443 when the CA connects using the acme-tls/1 ALPN protocol.

In ACME, a challenge token joined to the base64url-encoded JWK thumbprint of the account public key. Publishing it or its digest binds the challenge response to that account; signed ACME account requests separately prove possession of the private account key.
Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (RFC 7301): a TLS extension where client and server agree which application protocol, such as HTTP/2, runs over the connection.
Internet Engineering Task Force: the open standards body that develops internet protocols such as TLS, ACME and MLS and publishes them as RFCs.
A free, automated public CA run by the non-profit ISRG since 2015. It issues domain-validated certificates through ACME and is one of the largest CAs by volume.

Internet Security Research Group, the non-profit behind Let’s Encrypt. ISRG Root X1 is one of its root certificates; trust and usable certification paths depend on the client’s platform and trust-store version.
An older IdenTrust root that cross-signed Let's Encrypt so its certificates worked on old devices. It expired on 30 September 2021, breaking clients that could not build a path to ISRG Root X1.
A certificate whose SAN contains a name like *.example.com, which matches exactly one extra label (www.example.com, not a.b.example.com).

The part of the DNS namespace managed by one administrator, such as example.com and its records. Delegating just the _acme-challenge name lets automation answer challenges without control of the whole zone.
A DNS record holding arbitrary text, used for domain-ownership proofs such as ACME DNS-01 challenges and for email policies such as DMARC.
Announcing someone else's IP address range in BGP so that internet traffic for it is routed to the attacker, at least from some networks. A brief hijack can fool a CA's domain validation.
A CA repeating domain validation from several network locations and requiring a quorum to agree, so a routing attack that affects one region cannot pass validation on its own.
Certification Authority Authorization (RFC 8659): a DNS record listing which CAs may issue certificates for a domain. Compliant CAs must check it before issuing.
One CA signing another CA's certificate (with the same key and name as its self-signed root), so clients that trust only the older CA can still validate the newer one.
An industry body of certificate authorities and browser makers that sets the rules public TLS CAs must follow, including maximum certificate lifetimes.
The CA/Browser Forum's rules for issuing public TLS certificates: validation methods, key protection, lifetimes and audits. Root programmes require CAs to follow them.
A browser or operating-system vendor's process for deciding which root CAs to include in its trust store, and for auditing and removing them. Mozilla, Apple, Microsoft and Google each run one.

A Dutch certificate authority compromised in 2011, resulting in fraudulent certificates including one for Google’s domains and removal of browser trust. This definition concerns the documented security incident rather than later legal or financial outcomes.

Restricting a client’s accepted certificates or public keys beyond ordinary certification-path validation. A deployment needs a deliberate update and recovery plan; backup keys and CA pins change both resilience and the set of trusted signing powers.
HTTP Public Key Pinning (RFC 7469): a header that told browsers which keys a site would use. It was removed from browsers because a mistake could lock users out for months.

A certificate authority run by an organisation for its own services, devices and mutual TLS, trusted only by clients it configures. It gives control and short lifetimes but makes you responsible for the root key.

Infrastructure managing communication between services, often including identity, traffic policy and telemetry. Implementations can use per-workload proxies, shared node proxies or other designs; a sidecar is not inherent.
An open-source service mesh for Kubernetes. It issues each workload a short-lived certificate with a SPIFFE identity and rotates it automatically.
Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone: a standard for naming workloads with URIs such as spiffe://cluster/ns/shop/sa/api and putting them in certificates for mutual TLS.
Uniform Resource Identifier: a string naming a resource, such as https://example.com/ or spiffe://cluster/ns/shop. URLs are URIs that also say where to fetch something.

Client settings (Python verify=False or CERT_NONE, Go InsecureSkipVerify) that skip certificate checks. The connection is still encrypted, but to whoever answers, so a man-in-the-middle can read everything.

HTTP Strict Transport Security (RFC 6797): a browser policy requiring HTTPS for a host for a set time. Protection requires a previously accepted policy or a preload entry; an unprotected first visit can still be downgraded.
Server Name Indication: a TLS extension in which the client names the host it wants, so one IP address can serve several certificates. It is sent in clear unless ECH is used.

A public search service over Certificate Transparency data operated by Sectigo. It helps discover logged certificates, but search availability and indexing do not guarantee a complete instantaneous view.

aliases: unable to get local issuer certificate
definition: An OpenSSL/Python verification error indicating that an issuer needed to build an acceptable certificate path could not be found locally. Missing intermediates and differences in available trust anchors can cause path-building failures; diagnose the actual chain and trust store.

A TLS hybrid key-exchange group combining X25519 with ML-KEM-768 under a specified combiner. Its client share contains 32 bytes of X25519 public value plus a 1,184-byte ML-KEM encapsulation key; SSH uses a separate named hybrid construction.
In TLS 1.3, the public Diffie–Hellman (or KEM) value a side sends in its hello message for a chosen group.

Distinguishing cryptographic inputs for different roles or purposes with specified labels, prefixes or contexts. It prevents defined cross-use ambiguities when the encodings and assumptions hold; arbitrary external protocols must also avoid overlapping formats.
example: TLS 1.3 prefixes the signed transcript with 64 spaces and the string "TLS 1.3, server CertificateVerify".

definition: A fixed label such as "TLS 1.3, server CertificateVerify" included in signed or derived data to bind it to one protocol role and purpose.
A named combination of algorithms a TLS connection uses. In TLS 1.3 it names only the AEAD and hash, for example TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256; key exchange and signatures are negotiated separately.

The TLS extension indicating which signature algorithms a peer accepts, for example ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256 or rsa_pss_rsae_sha256. It appears in ClientHello and can also appear in a server’s CertificateRequest for client authentication.

TLS 1.3’s labelled HKDF expansion, which encodes the output length, a label prefixed with tls13 and a context. It can require multiple HMAC output blocks; deriving a short key or IV with SHA-256 needs one.
Produced deterministically but designed to be computationally indistinguishable from random data to an observer lacking the relevant secret state, under stated cryptographic assumptions.
In TLS 1.3, a per-direction secret from the key schedule from which the actual AEAD key and IV are expanded. There are separate ones for client and server, and for handshake and application data.
The TLS protocol version specified by RFC 5246 in 2008. It supports suites and negotiation options removed by TLS 1.3; older TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are distinct deprecated versions.

A TLS handshake confirmation message: an HMAC over the transcript hash keyed from the sending side’s handshake traffic secret. Successful verification authenticates that transcript and confirms possession of the corresponding secret; it does not mean both sides have already sent Finished.

Zero round-trip-time data: TLS 1.3 application data sent by a resuming client before receiving the new server flight. Its protection depends on the PSK, lacks fresh-DH forward secrecy and can be replayed; application-level replay safety requires more than merely labelling an operation idempotent.

TLS’s framing unit: a five-byte header followed by content or a protected record body. In TLS 1.3, content fragments are limited to 16 KiB; encrypted inner type, padding and AEAD expansion add overhead within separate bounds.
A unit of data: 1,000 bytes in SI usage (sometimes loosely used for 1,024 bytes, properly a kibibyte, KiB).
A unit of data: 1,000,000 bytes (10^6) in SI usage. MB/s means megabytes per second.
A counter numbering messages in order. In TLS 1.3 each direction keeps a 64-bit record counter, starting at 0 for each key, that is mixed into the nonce and never sent; TCP separately numbers bytes.

A TLS 1.3 post-handshake message advancing the sender’s application traffic secret and corresponding receiver secret. The new direction-specific key starts with sequence number zero; implementations must schedule updates before applicable limits.
The maximum amount of data or number of messages one key should protect before being replaced, set so an attacker's chance of breaking the cipher's guarantees stays negligible.
example: RFC 8446 limits AES-GCM to about 2^24.5 full-size records per key.

definition: A 2013 timing attack on TLS CBC suites: small processing-time differences caused by padding and MAC checks leaked plaintext.
Reconnecting to a TLS server using a PSK from an earlier session instead of a full certificate handshake, which saves computation and can save a round trip.
The TLS 1.3 secret, derived at the end of a handshake, from which the PSK for each session ticket is computed.
An opaque value a TLS server gives the client for later resumption. A stateless ticket holds the resumption state encrypted under a server-side ticket key; a stateful one is just a lookup ID.

A server-side key protecting stateless resumption-ticket state. If the recovered state reveals the PSK, later compromise can expose recorded PSK-only resumption and 0-RTT traffic; exact state formats vary.

TLS 1.3’s PSK-only key-establishment mode, with no fresh Diffie–Hellman contribution. Later PSK exposure breaks forward secrecy for that handshake; exposure of a ticket key matters when it reveals the required PSK state.

A TLS 1.3 PSK mode combining a PSK with fresh asymmetric key establishment, such as (EC)DHE in the classical example. It can use a resumption or external PSK. Fresh uncompromised key establishment protects 1-RTT traffic against later PSK-only compromise; 0-RTT does not get that property.
Encrypted Client Hello (RFC 9849, 2026): a TLS extension that encrypts the sensitive parts of the ClientHello, such as the server name, to a public key the server publishes, usually in DNS.
The first message of a TLS handshake: the client's supported versions, cipher suites, key shares, extensions and a random value. Without ECH it is sent unencrypted.

Ending a TLS connection at a server, proxy or load balancer that decrypts that TLS layer. Forwarded content needs its own protection where required; an already encrypted inner application payload may remain unreadable to the terminator.

Encryption applied separately to successive communication hops, with plaintext available at the hop terminators at that layer. TLS can provide such protection and can also carry an independently end-to-end encrypted payload.
The TLS alert sent when a received record fails AEAD authentication. The connection is then closed.

A TLS alert indicating that the sender will send no more messages on that connection. Its absence makes transport closure potentially truncated; application framing and policy are needed to assess completeness, and absence alone does not prove an attack.
A network device that inspects or modifies traffic in transit, such as a firewall or proxy. Middleboxes that misparse new protocol features can break deployments.

The mathematical group and parameters used by a Diffie–Hellman exchange. Security depends on the group structure, parameter size and validation, not simply a bit count; 512-bit finite-field export groups are insecure.
Everything involved in keeping keys safe through their life: generating, storing, distributing, using, rotating, revoking and destroying them, plus controlling and auditing who can use them.
The stages a cryptographic key passes through: generation, storage, distribution, use, rotation, and finally revocation and destruction. Each stage has its own failure modes.

HashiCorp’s secrets and key-management product, which can store encrypted secrets, issue dynamic credentials and expose cryptographic operations. Edition and source-licence terms vary; a product’s published source is not itself an open-source-licence claim.
Amazon's managed service for storing and rotating secrets such as database passwords and API keys, delivered to authorised workloads at runtime.

A cloud provider's key-management service (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault): keys live inside the service, applications call APIs to encrypt, decrypt or sign, and every call is checked against policy and can be logged.
example: AWS KMS symmetric Encrypt accepts at most 4,096 bytes of plaintext.

definition: A key marked so that the HSM or KMS will use it but never output it in plaintext. A compromised caller can still ask for operations with it while it has access.
Physical design that makes it hard to extract secrets from a device by opening, probing or manipulating it.

A cryptographic module’s configured reaction to detected tampering, which may include zeroisation of sensitive security parameters. Detection coverage and response requirements depend on the module and its validated security level.

A US cryptographic-module security standard with four security levels across defined areas. Requirements include roles, interfaces, physical protection and testing; a module’s certificate and security policy identify its validated configuration and scope.
The Payment Card Industry security standard for HSMs used in card payments, for example to process PINs and payment keys.
A standard C programming interface (also called Cryptoki) for talking to HSMs and smart cards: generate keys, sign, encrypt and set key attributes such as non-exportable.
Cryptography API: Next Generation: Windows's cryptographic interface, which can use keys held in software, a TPM or an HSM through key storage providers.
DNS Security Extensions: digital signatures on DNS records, checked along a chain from the root zone's key down, so resolvers can detect forged answers.
Key signing key: a DNSSEC key used to sign a zone’s DNSKEY set. The root KSK provides a widely used DNSSEC trust anchor, with its sensitive operations performed under IANA ceremony procedures.
The DNS record type that publishes a zone's DNSSEC public keys.
Android's hardware-backed keystore in a separate secure chip, which keeps keys away from the main processor.

Trusted Platform Module: a standardised hardware or firmware security component supporting protected keys, platform measurements and policy-bound operations. A TPM need not be a separate physical chip.

A family of Yubico hardware security keys supporting selected authentication and cryptographic applications, depending on model. On-device generated keys can resist plaintext export; imported keys may have copies elsewhere.
Data encryption key: the key that actually encrypts the data in envelope encryption, usually a fresh AES key per object, file or record, kept only in wrapped form at rest.

Key encryption key: a key used to protect other keys, such as wrapping and unwrapping DEKs in envelope encryption. Its custody and permitted operations depend on the system; separating key and bulk-data purposes is a design rule.

A data encryption key (DEK) stored in encrypted form: it has been encrypted ("wrapped") under a key-encryption key, usually one held inside a KMS or HSM. Unwrapping decrypts it again, which in a KMS needs permission to use that key.

In AWS KMS, a set of non-secret key–value pairs bound to a ciphertext as AEAD associated data. Decryption fails unless the same context is supplied, and it appears in CloudTrail logs, so it should never contain secrets.
example: Encrypting with {"user": "42"} means a ciphertext moved into user 99's row will not decrypt.

definition: The AWS KMS operation that returns a new data key twice: in plaintext for immediate use, and wrapped under a KMS key for storage.
Amazon Elastic Block Store: network disks for EC2 virtual machines, encrypted at rest with KMS-wrapped data keys.
Database encryption of data files at rest that is invisible to applications: the database decrypts automatically for any query it runs, so it protects stolen disks, not SQL injection.
Making encrypted data permanently unreadable by destroying every usable copy of its key, instead of finding and deleting every copy of the data itself.
Replacing a key with new key material so new data is protected by the new key. It limits how much data one key protects but does not, by itself, re-protect data a stolen old key can already decrypt.
example: AWS KMS automatic rotation creates new key material yearly by default but keeps old versions to decrypt old data.

definition: NIST’s GCM specification. Its IV uniqueness and invocation requirements depend on the IV construction; the random-IV construction has a total limit of 2 to the power 32 invocations per key across all devices, with additional message-length and authentication bounds.
NIST's Recommendation for Key Management: guidance on key types, lifecycles, cryptoperiods and protection.
Requiring two or more authorised people to act together for a sensitive operation, so no single insider can perform it.

A rule requiring participation by at least M of N designated holders, for example 3 of 7 smart-card holders to activate an HSM. It can tolerate absences and, when M is at least 2, prevent one holder acting alone.
A card with a secure chip that stores keys and performs cryptographic operations; HSM operators use them as physical credentials.
A scheme that splits a secret into N shares so that any M of them can rebuild it, while fewer than M reveal nothing.
example: Split a backup key into 5 shares with threshold 3: any 3 shareholders can recover it.

definition: A scripted, witnessed and recorded procedure for generating or using a very sensitive key, such as a root CA key or the DNSSEC root KSK.

aliases: Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers
definition: Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers: the non-profit that coordinates the DNS root and runs the DNSSEC root key ceremonies at two US facilities.
Automatically searching code repositories and commits for credentials such as API keys and private keys, so leaks are caught and the keys rotated.
A script Git runs before accepting a commit locally; it can block commits that contain secrets.
A component whose failure stops the whole system. Routing every request through one KMS region makes it one.
A cap a cloud service puts on how many API calls a client may make per second; exceeding it gets requests throttled or rejected.
Encrypting a whole drive or volume so its data is unreadable if the hardware is stolen. While the system runs, data is decrypted for anyone with legitimate access.
Amazon's client-side library implementing envelope encryption with KMS, including optional caching of data keys.
Social Security number: a US identifier issued by the Social Security Administration, commonly used as an example of sensitive personal data. It is not a general cryptographic credential.

Moving valid ciphertext into a different application context to obtain unauthorised acceptance. Authenticated associated data can reject the substitution when the application independently obtains and verifies the expected context.
End-to-end encryption: only the communicating devices hold the keys, so servers in between relay ciphertext they cannot read.
Meta's messaging app, which uses the Signal protocol for end-to-end encryption, Sender Keys for groups and key transparency for identity keys.
The property that a session becomes secure again after an attacker who stole its state loses access, once fresh secrets they do not know are mixed in. Also called break-in recovery or self-healing.

For shared-key message authentication, either key holder can produce a valid tag, so the tag alone is not transferable proof of which peer authored the message. Broader protocol deniability requires additional assumptions and does not decide legal evidence questions.

Extended Triple Diffie–Hellman: Signal's original session-start protocol. Alice combines her identity and ephemeral keys with Bob's uploaded prekeys in three or four Diffie–Hellman computations, so she can start encrypting while Bob is offline.
A public key a messaging client uploads to the server in advance, so others can start an encrypted session with it while it is offline.
The set of public keys a server hands out for a user: identity key, signed prekey with its signature, and (if available) one one-time prekey.

A long-term key pair representing an endpoint or user identity in a messaging design. Public keys authenticate prekeys and contribute to identity comparisons; private-key custody, backup and device sharing depend on the protocol and deployment.
A medium-term Diffie–Hellman key in X3DH, signed with the owner's identity key and replaced periodically (for example weekly or monthly).

A prepublished public key intended for one session start, with its private half retained by the endpoint until the initial message is successfully processed and then deleted. A server can misbehave, so distribution and replay assumptions still matter.
Both parties proving to each other which keys they hold, rather than only the server proving its identity.

Post-Quantum Extended Diffie–Hellman: Signal’s asynchronous hybrid key-agreement protocol, adding a post-quantum KEM contribution to classical DH contributions. The published revision aims at post-quantum forward secrecy but its mutual authentication still relies on classical discrete-log hardness.
A key-update mechanism that only moves forward: each step derives new keys with a one-way function and deletes the old ones, so stolen current keys do not reveal earlier ones.
The half of the Double Ratchet that turns a chain key through a one-way KDF for every message, producing a message key and the next chain key.

The Double Ratchet mechanism that mixes new Diffie–Hellman contributions into the root key to create new message-key chains. Recovery requires attacker access to end and fresh contributions unknown to the attacker to be successfully processed.
In the Double Ratchet, a 32-byte secret per direction that is advanced once per message to produce that message's key, then replaced.
In the Double Ratchet, the one-off key that encrypts a single message, derived from the chain key and deleted after use.
In the Double Ratchet, the long-running secret that each new Diffie–Hellman output is mixed into, producing a new root key and a fresh chain key.
The Diffie–Hellman public key a Double Ratchet sender attaches to each message. A new one from the peer triggers a DH ratchet step.
Message keys a receiver derives and stores for messages that have not arrived yet, so late or out-of-order messages can still be decrypted. They are capped because stored keys weaken forward secrecy.

Sparse Post-Quantum Ratchet: Signal’s post-quantum ratcheting design announced in 2025. It is combined with the elliptic-curve Double Ratchet in the Triple Ratchet; the two are related constructions rather than interchangeable names.
A short hash of a public key (or keys) shown to humans for comparison, so a substituted key is noticed.
A two-dimensional barcode a phone camera can read; messaging apps use them to compare safety numbers quickly.

An auditable directory design providing verifiable evidence about identity-key mappings over time. Detecting inconsistent views depends on client proof verification and the system’s monitoring or consistency assumptions; it does not establish a key’s real-world owner by itself.
An attack where a key directory (such as a messaging server) gives a victim the attacker's public key in place of the real contact's, then relays messages in the middle.
Signal's algorithm for managing sessions across a user's multiple devices, including per-user or per-device identity keys.
Sending one message to many recipients. In Sender Keys, the sender encrypts once and the server delivers copies to every group member.

A group-messaging design distributing each sender’s chain key through pairwise sessions so that a message can be encrypted once for the group. Deleted past chain/message keys support forward secrecy; recovery needs fresh sender keys distributed over channels the attacker can no longer read.

Messaging Layer Security, standardised in RFC 9420: a protocol for authenticated end-to-end encrypted groups. Its tree can give logarithmic update paths in favourable balanced states; actual ciphertext and processing costs depend on tree resolutions and membership changes.

The tree-based key-update mechanism used by MLS. Members hold the private material for their leaf and certain nodes on the path to the root, while blank nodes and unmerged leaves affect which keys and ciphertexts an update needs.
An MLS tree node that has no stored public-key value, for example after certain removal operations. Resolving blank nodes can require traversing descendants, which changes update size and work.
A binary tree whose height is kept close to the minimum for its size. A full balanced tree has logarithmic height; a generic binary tree need not be balanced or shallow.
example: A balanced binary tree with 4,096 leaves is 12 levels deep.

definition: Commercial spyware from NSO Group that compromises phones and reads messages after the app decrypts them, so end-to-end encryption does not help.
Malware that secretly monitors a device, such as reading messages, location or keystrokes.

A Signal message-delivery design reducing explicit sender identity exposed to the service by encrypting sender information for the recipient. It does not promise anonymity against timing, network-address or other metadata analysis.
Inferring information from communication patterns, such as who talks to whom, when, how often and how much, without reading the content.
A numeric address identifying an interface in an IP network. A service sees the connecting peer’s network address, which may belong to a NAT, VPN or proxy rather than identify the originating person.

Notation giving an asymptotic upper bound on growth with input size, ignoring constant factors. A linear-time algorithm is also bounded above by larger polynomial bounds, so Big O alone does not assert an exact growth rate.
example: A populated balanced MLS tree has logarithmic path depth; that alone does not bound every update’s total work or bytes.

definition: In GCM, the secret value H (the encryption of a zero block) that the GHASH polynomial uses to compute tags. Nonce reuse can let an attacker solve for it and then forge tags.

The GCM nonce-reuse attack family associated with Joux: repeated key/nonce observations create algebraic relations involving the authentication subkey and can enable forgery. Exact recovery and usable forgeries depend on the observed messages.
Key Reinstallation Attacks (2017): manipulating WPA2 handshake messages so a device reinstalls a key in use and resets its nonce counter, causing nonce reuse.
Wi-Fi Protected Access 2: the Wi-Fi security standard from 2004, succeeded by WPA3.
Microsoft's web framework. In 2010 a padding oracle in how it encrypted cookies and view state let attackers decrypt and forge them (bulletin MS10-070).
The broken construction of hashing a secret key followed by the message with a plain hash such as SHA-256, and using the result as a tag. It falls to length-extension attacks; use HMAC.
Python's general-purpose random module, built on the Mersenne Twister. It is fine for simulations and games but must never be used for passwords, tokens or keys.

Unpredictable input, such as hardware noise or timing jitter, that a random generator collects before producing keys. A device that generates keys before gathering enough of it can produce predictable or repeated keys.

An operating-system identifier for a running process. The available range and allocation policy depend on the platform and configuration; predictable small identifiers are unsuitable as the sole secret seed for key generation.

A device normally operated without a directly attached display, keyboard or mouse. Some devices studied in shared-RSA-factor research had inadequate early-boot randomness; being headless alone does not imply a weak RNG.
A side-channel attack that measures how long memory accesses take to learn which table entries secret-dependent code used, revealing keys from table-lookup AES or naive RSA.

Secret-dependent division-timing vulnerabilities disclosed in implementations of the Kyber KEM around the start of 2024. Kyber and final ML-KEM are related algorithms with distinct specifications; the finding concerns affected implementations.

A computer that uses quantum states (qubits) to run certain algorithms, such as Shor's, exponentially faster than classical machines. One large and fault-tolerant enough to break RSA or elliptic curves does not yet exist.
Running time that grows like a fixed power of the input size, such as n³, rather than exponentially. Problems solvable in polynomial time are considered efficiently solvable.

The US National Security Agency’s Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0, announced in 2022 for national security systems. It includes AES-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512, post-quantum key establishment and signatures, and LMS or XMSS for software/firmware signing; algorithm names and transition requirements must be checked against the applicable suite revision.
The US National Security Agency, which sets cryptographic requirements for US national security systems.
Michele Mosca's rule of thumb x + y > z: if data's secrecy lifetime (x) plus migration time (y) exceeds the time until a quantum computer exists (z), you should already be migrating.

Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, standardised in FIPS 205 in 2024 from SPHINCS+. Its security relies on specified hash-function properties, with larger signatures and parameter-dependent performance compared with many lattice-signature choices.
example: SLH-DSA-128s has a 32-byte public key and a 7,856-byte signature.

definition: A digital signature construction based on specified security properties of hash functions, such as SLH-DSA. State management, signature sizes and other requirements depend on the construction; hash-based does not eliminate implementation or key-custody risks.
Cryptography based on hard problems over high-dimensional lattices of points, such as finding short vectors. No efficient quantum attack is known; ML-KEM and ML-DSA are lattice-based.
FFT over NTRU-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, from Falcon: a compact lattice signature that NIST is standardising as FIPS 206.

Hamming Quasi-Cyclic: a code-based KEM selected by NIST in March 2025 for standardisation to diversify post-quantum key-establishment assumptions. Selection is distinct from publication of a final standard.
Public-key cryptography built on the difficulty of decoding error-correcting codes, such as HQC and Classic McEliece.
Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation: a post-quantum KEM candidate broken in 2022 by a classical attack; the original attack recovered a SIKEp434 key in about an hour on a single core.
The function that merges the secrets of a hybrid key exchange into one key, designed so the output stays secret if either input does.

An open implementation of SSH. Its 9.0 release introduced a default Streamlined NTRU Prime/X25519 hybrid in 2022, and 10.0 selected mlkem768x25519-sha256 by default in 2025; enabled algorithms still depend on configuration.
A family of lattice-based key-encapsulation designs distinct from the original NTRU family. OpenSSH has combined Streamlined NTRU Prime sntrup761 with X25519 in a hybrid key exchange.

Apple’s iMessage post-quantum protocol announced in 2024, combining classical elliptic-curve and post-quantum contributions during session setup and rekeying. The original design describes Kyber; draft Kyber and final ML-KEM encodings must not be assumed interchangeable.

A proposed (IETF draft) form of X.509 certificate that builds Certificate-Transparency-style public logging into issuance: the CA commits to many certificates in one Merkle tree, so up-to-date clients can check a short inclusion proof instead of several large post-quantum signatures.

The amount of TCP data permitted before acknowledgements expand or otherwise change the initial sending allowance. RFC 6928 permits an increased initial window up to ten segments within its stated bounds; actual configuration and pacing determine handshake effects.

Maximum Segment Size: the maximum TCP payload advertised for a connection direction. With a 1,500-byte IPv4 path and minimum 20-byte IP and TCP headers, 1,460 bytes is a common example; IP version, options, tunnels and path MTU change the usable payload.

The ability to migrate cryptographic algorithms, parameters and implementations with controlled changes across a system. Configuration and modular interfaces can help, but compatibility, stored data and external dependencies may still require coordinated migration.

NIST’s November 2024 initial public draft on transition to post-quantum standards. It proposes deprecation after 2030 for listed 112-bit-strength classical uses, such as RSA-2048 and P-224, and disallowance after 2035 for listed quantum-vulnerable uses; P-256 provides about 128-bit classical security, not 112-bit.
A reminder a user stores with their password. Stored unencrypted next to encrypted passwords, hints help attackers guess the passwords.
A basic cryptographic building block, such as a hash function, block cipher, MAC, signature or key exchange. Protocols such as TLS combine primitives.

Key material scoped to a connection or protocol session rather than a long-term identity. Its compromise impact depends on derivation relationships, reuse and retained state; the name alone does not guarantee isolation from other sessions.
A multivariate post-quantum signature scheme that reached the final round of NIST's competition and was broken classically in 2022 (Beullens, "Breaking Rainbow takes a weekend on a laptop").
A notice a messaging app shows when a contact's identity key changes, for example after a new phone, so users can re-verify safety numbers in case it is an attack.

A message/signature/public-key combination accepted by the scheme’s verification algorithm. Under its assumptions this provides evidence of access to signing authority; it does not by itself establish a human identity, freshness or freedom from key compromise.

Encrypting stored plaintext again under new key material, often after decryption of an earlier ciphertext. It can protect current copies from future use of a stolen old key, but cannot retract plaintext or old ciphertext/key copies already obtained by an attacker.
Messages arriving in a different order from the one they were sent in, common on mobile networks. Protocols must either reject or correctly handle late arrivals.

A party or algorithm checking a digital signature against a message and public key without needing signing authority. Certificate-path validation additionally checks trust, constraints and policy; it is more than one signature check.
example: A browser acting as a certificate verifier checks the server certificate chain up to a root in its trust store before trusting the TLS handshake.

definition: Software applying a certificate-validation policy, including a trust store, issuer path, validity, constraints and application identity rules. Directly checking one issuer signature is only part of this process.
A SAML element identifying a subject using a defined format. A handler must use the identity from the assertion it actually validated rather than an untrusted document-wide lookup.

Signal’s composition combining message-key contributions from an elliptic-curve Double Ratchet and a Sparse Post-Quantum Ratchet. Delivery and fresh-secret assumptions govern forward secrecy and recovery.

TLS 1.3 application traffic using the regular post-handshake traffic keys. With fresh ephemeral DH it gains guarantees unavailable to PSK-only 0-RTT early data, subject to the authentication and key-erasure assumptions.
The TLS version originally specified by RFC 2246. RFC 8996 formally deprecates it; it is distinct from TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
The TLS version specified by RFC 4346. RFC 8996 formally deprecates it; deployments should enforce a supported minimum protocol version.
The earlier NIST cryptographic-module security standard succeeded by FIPS 140-3. Module validation status and transition rules must be checked for the relevant implementation and date.
An SSH key-exchange method combining ML-KEM-768 and X25519 with its specified hash-based derivation. It became OpenSSH’s default in release 10.0; it is not the TLS X25519MLKEM768 wire format.

The actual symmetric AEAD key used to encrypt or decrypt records for one TLS direction and phase. It is expanded, along with a separate IV, from a traffic secret; the key and its parent traffic secret are distinct values.

A private/public Diffie–Hellman key pair maintained by a Double Ratchet endpoint. Its public half is sent in message headers; its private half remains local and is needed for DH. A public ratchet key alone is not the pair.

A logical key resource in a key-management service, including its identifier, metadata, policy and cryptographic material or reference to that material. A resource can retain multiple material versions; the key resource is distinct from the KMS service providing operations.
